props.title: Quick Change

sections.content: Quick Change stands as Bill Murray's only directorial effort (co-directed with Howard Franklin), and it's a criminally underrated heist comedy that captures New York City's chaotic spirit perfectly. Murray plays Grimm, a burned-out city planner who executes a brilliant bank robbery while dressed as a clown, only to find that escaping NYC proves infinitely harder than the heist itself. The film follows a similar DNA to After Hours (1985) and The Out-of-Towners (1970), where the city itself becomes an antagonist, throwing increasingly absurd obstacles at our protagonists.

sections.content: The film brilliantly subverts the heist genre by placing its focus on the escape rather than the robbery. While movies like Dog Day Afternoon (1975) and Inside Man (2006) spend their runtime on elaborate heist mechanics, Quick Change dispenses with the robbery in its first act, then transforms into a desperate comedy of errors. Murray's deadpan excellence finds perfect foils in Geena Davis and Randy Quaid, creating a trio whose mounting frustration mirrors many New Yorkers' daily experiences.

The film's influence can be seen in later urban chaos comedies like Date Night (2010) and Game Night (2018), where ordinary people face escalating city-based mishaps. But Quick Change stands apart for its bitter sweetness about New York - a love-hate letter to a city that's simultaneously magnificent and maddening. The film's commentary on urban decay and bureaucratic dysfunction remains surprisingly relevant today. SUBHEAD: Urban Chaos and Comedy

sections.content: What makes Quick Change special is how it captures the particular absurdity of city life. Like The Taking of Pelham One Two Three (1974) and Trading Places (1983), it understands that New York's real character lies not in its landmarks but in its everyday lunacy - construction detours, language barriers, and Byzantine regulations that seem designed to drive people mad. Murray and Franklin's direction emphasizes this through wide shots that make their characters look tiny against the looming urban landscape.
